Industry observers note that to investigate the optical properties of the fabricated structures, we performed momentum-resolved photoluminescence and reflectivity measurements (Methods). The corresponding maps for both transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) polarizations and different pitches are shown in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. The momentum-resolved photoluminescence, obtained by spatially selecting the emission from one grating, is shown in Fig. 1f for TE polarization. Two strongly coupled modes are clearly visible (yellow solid lines), which we attribute to the fundamental (TE0) and first-order (TE1) lower polariton waveguide modes. Although the upper polariton branch is not visible31,32,33, the characteristic dispersion of the waveguide modes, which is approximated as linear in the weak coupling regime (white dashed lines), highlights an increasing bending approaching the exciton resonance, providing clear evidence of the strong radiation-matter coupling. Reflectivity and photoluminescence data were fitted using a two-coupled-oscillator model yielding Rabi splitting energies of Ω = 140 ± 10 meV for both the TE1 and TE0 modes (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6), consistent with previous reports23,34. The presence of these two modes is compatible with a waveguide thickness ranging between 250 nm and 290 nm, as confirmed by finite-difference time-domain simulations presented in Extended Data Fig. 1 for different grating pitches. It is key to note that the TE1 mode appears brighter because one of its electric-field maxima lies closer to the top surface of the waveguide, where the grating is patterned, resulting in more efficient coupling to free-space radiation and a larger momentum-space linewidth. The typical real-space photoluminescence emission is shown in the right part of Fig. 1f and the exciton/photon fraction for LPB1 is reported in Supplementary Fig. 8.

In the absence of external optical resonators, lasing in perovskite microstructures can arise from optical feedback provided by sharp crystal facets acting as Fabry–Pérot cavities.23,24,35,36. In waveguide geometries, this feedback occurs predominantly in the transverse direction23, thus proving ineffective for photonic integrated circuits, which normally demand longitudinal propagation. Moreover, this lasing emission lacks spectral tunability, as it is governed by the intrinsic balance between optical gain and loss within the material. Alternative strategies based on isolated perovskite blocks evanescently coupled to active waveguides24 can promote in-plane propagation, but are limited by weak field overlap and inefficient coupling. Longitudinal polariton lasing assisted by integrated grating reflectors was demonstrated in a GaAs-based waveguide at cryogenic temperature17 and in gallium nitride (GaN)-based waveguide at room temperature37. However, in these systems the lasing mode remains confined within the reflective elements, without efficiently coupling into a propagating waveguide mode. By contrast, our approach integrates tunable lasing emission within a guided architecture, providing a direct route towards integrated polaritonic circuits. Moreover, it is achieved through a simple, scalable growth process yielding waveguides with embedded couplers, unlike the more complex fabrication required for GaAs or GaN platforms.

To verify the formation of such a longitudinal optical feedback, the perovskite waveguide was off-resonantly pumped between two couplers. The real-space TE-polarized photoluminescence maps at excitation powers (P) below (left) and above (right) the lasing threshold (Pth) are shown in Fig. 2a. At low pumping power, the two outcouplers are barely visible, as only a relatively small portion of the emitted light is effectively coupled into the waveguide modes. By contrast, at high excitation power, a pronounced signal emerges from both outcouplers, suggesting that a longitudinal feedback is taking place. Notably, the lasing signal extracted from the grating disappears in TM polarization (Supplementary Fig. 9), confirming the polarization sensitivity of the feedback mechanism. To further investigate the onset and evolution of the lasing emission, we performed a real-space energy-resolved measurement and evaluated the emitted intensity (Extended Data Fig. 2) collected from one of the two outcouplers for the lasing signal (integrated between 2.31 eV and 2.32 eV), as shown in Fig. 2b. A clear threshold is observed at roughly Pth = 55 µJ cm−2, consistent with previous reports on similar perovskite materials19,35,38,39. The transition is accompanied by a clear linewidth narrowing as reported in the inset. The energy-resolved momentum-space maps are shown in Fig. 2c for the below-threshold (left panel) and above-threshold (right panel) regimes, and the corresponding kx–ky maps are reported in Supplementary Fig. 10.

a, Real-space image of a Fabry–Pérot in-plane cavity formed by two gratings (highlighted by the dashed squares); below threshold (left) the emission is dominated by exciton recombination under the pump spot, whereas above threshold (right) the lasing mechanism takes place and the emission from the two gratings is stronger than the photoluminescence not coupled to the guided mode. b, Emitted intensity integrated at the grating position from real-space energy-resolved measurements as a function of pumping fluence. Data points are obtained from three consecutive power-dependence measurements performed on the same structure as shown in blue, green and orange dots. The black points represent the average of the three power-dependence measurements. Dashed black lines are guides for the eye. The inset reveals the linewidth below (black line) and above threshold (red line) obtained from energy-resolved momentum-space measurements. c, Corresponding energy-resolved momentum-space emission below (left) and above threshold (right). The white dashed lines indicate the TE0 and TE1 polariton modes propagating downward (dashed lines) and upward (solid line). d, Lasing emission from three different cavities formed by couples of gratings having different pitches (270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, respectively); when the pitch is modified the energy of the lasing energy shifts. Scale bars, 5 μm.

Lasing occurs where longitudinal feedback selects a single mode due to the balance between gain and losses taking place at the reflectivity maximum induced by the grating, where losses are minimal. This point38,40 is slightly red-shifted and momentum-shifted with respect to the bandgap because finite-size and thickness variation in the grating profile cause new loss-favoured grating-to-waveguide backreflections15, as discussed in Supplementary Fig. 11. Lasing modes show a clear blueshift with increasing power, and more Fabry–Pérot modes emerge within the same spectral region (Extended Data Fig. 3). Notably, our configuration does not rely on large reflectivity or a strongly developed stop band; rather, a small but finite reflectivity is sufficient to enable cavity formation and mode selection, owing to the excellent gain properties of CsPbBr3. To demonstrate the spectral tunability of the lasing emission, we have tuned the periodicity within the integrated couplers by keeping their mutual distance constant. As shown in Fig. 2d, for three different grating geometries with pitches of 270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, a progressive blueshift is induced from roughly 2.28 eV to 2.315 eV. The below-threshold and above-threshold dispersions for all the measured gratings are reported in Extended Data Fig. 4. It is important to note that in the present device geometry, longitudinal feedback from the grating couplers coexist with transverse feedback from the waveguide edges. Above-threshold spatially resolved measurements confirm this coexistence, showing a roughly doubled mode spacing for edge emission, consistent with two cavity lengths of roughly 25 μm and 10 μm, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 12). Efficient propagation of the lasing signal along the waveguide allows its collection from the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element (Extended Data Fig. 6). From these data, together with further resonant propagation measurements, we estimate propagation losses, outcoupler attenuation and optical gain (Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14).

It has been revealed that in the following section we demonstrate another key functionality of our system: the optical amplification, which has not been previously achieved in similar polaritonic platforms at room temperature. This is essential for integrated photonic circuits as it compensates for propagation and coupling losses, thus enabling efficient on-chip light transport. We resonantly injected a pulsed beam (signal) through the input grating on the LPB1 mode and monitored the transmitted signal at the output located 25 µm away. A second pulsed beam (amplifier) was off-resonantly exciting the centre of the waveguide between two outcouplers where it generates an incoherent exciton population, as schematically shown in Fig. 3a. The signal beam was kept in the linear regime, thereby avoiding self-phase-modulation effects41 (Supplementary Fig. 15). We recorded the output intensity by scanning the time delay between the two pulses, keeping the signal with a constant intensity and changing the fluence of the amplifier. Figure 3b indicates the collected intensity as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, indicated by the blue, orange and green curves, respectively (Methods). At low pump fluences, the output signal remains unchanged, whereas at higher amplifier fluences it is strongly enhanced at 0 delay (Δt = 0 ps) and then decays within roughly 50 ps, demonstrating amplification once a sufficient particle density is reached. The decay follows a single-exponential fit with a characteristic time of 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, more than 1 order of magnitude shorter than the bare photoluminescence decay (Supplementary Fig. 16). To further explain the effect, power-dependent measurements at Δt = 0 ps were performed, as shown in Fig. 3c. Here the bottom panel represents the photoluminescence intensity generated by the off-resonant amplifier alone, which increases quadratically with pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 17), whereas the top panel corresponds to the intensity measured in the presence of both the signal and the amplifier beams, showing clear amplification with a marked threshold-like behaviour. This trend confirms optical amplification and is consistent with stimulated emission, where the probe stimulates particles from the incoherent exciton reservoir created by the amplifier, possibly assisted by acoustic phonons, recently shown to play a key role in perovskites42. The amplification threshold is found to occur at roughly Pth,Amp = 10 μJ cm−2, that is, well below the lasing threshold.

It has been revealed that a, Sketch of the integrated optical circuit used to measure polariton amplification: the off-resonant beam (amplifier) creates an exciton reservoir whereas the resonant beam (signal) excites a polariton state propagating along the waveguide. At the output grating the signal is amplified (amplified signal) thanks to stimulation from the exciton reservoir. Amplifier energy is Eamplifier = 2.58 eV in all the measurements. b, Collected intensity of the amplified signal as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2; black dashed line indicate the exponential fit. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.31 eV. A positive Δt corresponds to the case in which the signal arrives after the non-resonant pump, allowing amplification to take place while the reservoir is present. The decay time, 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, is the average of the exponential-fit values obtained at pump fluences of 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, which yield 22.1 ± 1.4 ps and 18.8 ± 0.9 ps, respectively. c, Power-dependent measurements at time delay 0 ps. Bottom: green dots represent the intensity of the amplifier alone; top, orange dots show the intensity of the amplified signal as a function of the amplifier fluence. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.26 eV. The horizontal error bars represent the power fluctuations of the amplifier, whereas the vertical error bars reflect the standard deviation derived from the signal evaluation across slightly different spectral regions, providing an estimate of the systematic uncertainty. d, Amplification factor as a function of the signal energy for two different amplifier fluences (P1 = 25 μJ cm−2 and P2 = 35 μJ cm−2) as indicated in c by the blue and red dashed lines. The amplification closely follows the photoluminescence spectral profile, increasing with the photoluminescence intensity. The photoluminescence spectrum, shown in arbitrary units, is included for qualitative comparison.

To test the spectral efficiency, we selected two amplifier fluences (P1 and P2, blue and red dashed vertical lines in Fig. 3c), both kept between the amplification and the lasing threshold, and scanned the signal energy, keeping its fluence constant. Figure 3d demonstrates the amplification factor as a function of the signal energy, defined as \(A=\frac{({S}_{{\rm{out}}}-{A}_{0})}{{S}_{0}}\), where Sout is the total output signal, and A0 and S0 are the independently measured amplifier and signal contributions, respectively. Clear amplification is observed over a broad energy range, with a superlinear dependence on signal energy and increasing spectral efficiency due to more efficient scattering and reduced group velocity, which enhances the interaction time with the reservoir. Crucially, amplification is observed even at energies well outside the narrow spectral region where lasing occurs (Supplementary Fig. 18) thus ruling out a cavity-mode feeding mechanism, which would instead be confined to the narrow spectral region defined by the lasing modes. In Supplementary Fig. 19, we present representative real-space maps of the signal, the amplifier and the amplified signal. Moreover, at the highest signal energy for which propagation is still sustained in the system the amplification factor approaches two orders of magnitude. Taking into account the spatial extension of the reservoir (Supplementary Fig. 18), we estimate the optical gain within a simple one-dimensional model as g = ln(A)/L, where A is the measured amplification factor and L is the effective interaction length, approximated by the amplifier full-width at half-maximum (13–15 µm). This yields values in the range of 5 × 102–3 × 103 cm−1 depending on the signal energy. Moreover, above the lasing threshold, the amplified signal saturates (Extended Data Fig. 7), consistent with reservoir depletion induced by the self-oscillating mode. Combining room-temperature operation with liquid-phase synthesis, our results represent a great advance over GaAs-based or ZnO-based platforms, which instead require cryogenic operation and demanding epitaxial growth16,43. In addition, the strong-coupling regime enables amplification through bosonic stimulation rather than population inversion, allowing operation at lower pump powers than conventional gain media.

We then exploit the complex geometries enabled by our fabrication approach to demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton system. A resonant signal beam (Eres = 2.265 eV) is injected through the input grating, propagates along the structure and is subsequently split into the two arms of an interferometric Y-splitter. At the end of each arm, the waveguide edges act as outcouplers, allowing for the formation of an interference pattern in the momentum space, directly accessing the relative phase difference between the two arms. A non-resonant pulse is then introduced in only one arm of the Y-splitter. A schematic of the configuration is shown in Fig. 4a, and the reflectivity image of the Y-splitter termination and the corresponding outcoupled signal are shown in Fig. 4b. A representative momentum-space map recorded with only the propagating signal highlights the expected interference pattern (Fig. 4c), whose origin is confirmed by selectively removing one output from the detection path (Supplementary Fig. 20). We then monitor the interference fringe shift as a function of the phase-shifter pulse energy at zero delay Δt = 0 ps between the optical shifter and the propagating signal beam. As shown in Fig. 4d, where the intensity profile along kx is plotted as a function of the optical-shifter fluence, a pronounced shift is generated. The phase shift, extracted from sinusoidal fits of the interferograms, reaches up to 2π with increasing pump pulse energy (Fig. 4e). As a consistency check, moving the phase-shifter beam to the opposite arm reverses the fringe shift direction (Extended Data Fig. 8), whereas amplification is observed only in the pumped arm (Supplementary Fig. 21). We model the experiment using two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance, as described in the Methods. At fixed probe frequency, this shift produces a change in the polariton wavevector and the corresponding phase accumulated over the propagation length is reported in Fig. 4f as a function of the exciton resonance shift.

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic of the Y-splitter device with an integrated input grating used to split a propagating resonant signal inside the structure while a non-resonant phase shifter (EPS = 2.58 eV) is applied only on one of its two arms. The ends of the two arms outcouple the propagating signal and behave as spatially separated coherent emitters, generating an interference pattern in momentum space that provides direct access to the relative phase. b, Real-space image of the Y-splitter termination (top) and the corresponding outcoupled signal (bottom) when only the resonant beam is present. c, Representative momentum-space map showing the interference pattern arising from coherent out-coupling of the two arms. d, Evolution of the interference fringes for increasing phase-shifter fluence. The direction of the fringe shift is highlighted by the black arrow. Bottom black profile represents the signal alone. Note that the incident pulse energy per operation is used here as the relevant metric (rather than fluence), as appropriate for single-device operation. The device footprint is roughly 20 μm2. e, Phase shift as a function of energy per pulse, showing a continuous increase reaching 2π. f, Calculated phase shift considering two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance. Scale bars, 2 μm (b), 1.5 μm–1 (c).

Finally, after establishing the presence of a suitable π-phase shift in the Y-splitter geometry, we extend this functionality to a full Mach–Zehnder interferometer. The polariton mode is resonantly excited at 2.265 eV through the input grating, while the transmitted signal is collected at the output, with the phase shifter applied to one arm of the interferometer, as illustrated in Fig. 5a,b. The output intensity is extracted from a fixed spatial region at the grating outcoupler and is shown in Fig. 5c after background subtraction (Supplementary Fig. 22). As the phase-shifter energy increases, the signal evolves from a maximum to a minimum and then back to a maximum, demonstrating a full 2π response well reproduced by a sine-squared fit. Notably, this sizable phase shift is achieved within an ultra-compact guided footprint (roughly 20 µm2, Fig. 5b), compared with millimetre-scale lithium-niobate phase shifters44,45. The large modulation is enabled by the polaritonic nature of the guided mode that enhances the nonlinear response to the pump-induced reservoir. Beyond its compactness, the direct use of polaritonic nonlinearities, with a residual contribution from the excitonic reservoir due to the off-resonant excitation, offers a route towards ultrafast integrated circuitry compared with thermo-optic nonlinearities46,47,48.

Recent findings suggest that a, Microscope image of the Mach–Zehnder interferometer with an integrated input and output grating. b, Example of the experimental configuration adopted: a resonant beam with a full-width at half-maximum comparable to the size of the grating coupler is focused on the input grating (left, signal input), propagates along the structure and is outcoupled at the output grating (right, signal output). The phase-shifter beam was pumping one arm of the interferometer. The images of the signal input, phase shifter and signal output regions were acquired separately and subsequently rescaled in intensity. c, Signal output as a function of the phase-shifter energy: black dots represent the experimental data, and the red line indicates the fitted curve. The data are collected at Δt = 0 ps, corresponding to temporal synchronization between the travelling signal beam and the phase-shifter beam at the phase-shifter spatial position. Scale bars, 10 μm.

In summary, we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polariton waveguide platform operating at room temperature, combining strong nonlinear propagation, tunable polariton lasing, optical amplification and nonlinear phase control within a single device. Our approach introduces a hybrid and high-throughput soft-lithography method that combines surface-tension–guided assembly with microfluidics, enabling single-step direct fabrication of active waveguides with integrated grating couplers. This provides a straightforward, cost-effective and scalable route for realizing self-assembled complex polaritonic architectures without the need for specialized vacuum equipment or epitaxial reactors. The developed architecture supports on-chip polariton lasing, with wavelength-selective emission enabled by longitudinal feedback from the integrated gratings and efficient propagation along the waveguide. Beyond lasing, we demonstrate room-temperature amplification of guided polariton signals by nearly two orders of magnitude. The threshold-like amplification and nonlinear response suggest potential for neuromorphic polariton devices, in which tailored excitation geometries and pulse sequences could enable neuron-like operations such as signal integration and threshold-triggered emission.

Furthermore, we demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton configuration, achieving phase shifts exceeding π within an ultra-compact footprint. Crucially, we harness this capability in a fully integrated Mach–Zehnder interferometer, enabling direct conversion of phase modulation into intensity modulation. The ability to coherently control the phase of propagating signals, combined with intrinsic ultrafast polaritonic nonlinearities, establishes this platform as a promising route towards ultrafast on-chip interferometric devices. These features—combining room-temperature operation, material tunability, scalable and cost-effective fabrication, and rich nonlinear functionalities—establish perovskite polariton waveguides as a versatile and promising platform for next-generation integrated photonic and polaritonic technologies.

The grating and waveguide nanostructures and microstructures were fabricated on 25 × 25 mm Si(100) substrates using EBL (RAITH Voyager) followed by reactive ion etching. The grating pattern was defined using a 130-nm-thick poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) electron-beam resist layer spin-coated onto the silicon substrate and exposed by EBL at a dose of 580 μC cm−2. The exposed resist was developed in a MIBK:IPA (1:3) solution. A 40-nm-thick chromium film, serving as an etch hard mask, was subsequently deposited by electron-beam evaporation, and the remaining resist was removed in acetone. The pattern was transferred for 50 nm into the silicon substrate using fluorine-based reactive ion etching (CF4, CHF3, O2, Ar). The chromium mask was then removed by wet chemical etching. An analogous process was used for the fabrication of the waveguide structures, with optimized parameters as follows: PMMA resist thickness of 360 nm, EBL exposure dose of 280 μC cm−2, chromium mask thickness of 60 nm and reactive ion etching etching depth of 250 nm. Following chromium mask removal, the silicon master was cleaned in a piranha solution for 15 min to eliminate any residual organic contamination. The final silicon master featured microwire waveguides and interferometer-like geometries with lateral dimensions from 2 µm to 30 µm, and a height of 250 nm. Each waveguide incorporated nanometre-scale grating arrays covering areas of roughly 10 × 10 µm2, with a height of 50 nm, pitches between 240 nm and 300 nm and varying filling factors, directly etched onto the surface. The aspect ratios (height/width) of the patterned structures, including both the waveguides and the gratings, ranged from approximately 0.01 to 0.60. The grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4), so that the grating lines remain confined within the inner region of the waveguide and do not overlap with the waveguide borders in the etch mask, thereby avoiding local sidewall indentations during the two-step dry-etching process and preserving a more uniform waveguide geometry for crystal growth. For the interferometer, the structure includes a sequence of lateral modulations before the Y-splitter, efficiently redistributing the guided mode into the two branches (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Industry observers note that perovskite devices were fabricated using a modified soft-lithography approach that combined surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing of a liquid precursor solution, using PDMS replicas moulded from silicon masters with predefined multiscale geometries. A mixture of PDMS prepolymer and curing agent (10:1, Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was cast onto the Si master and cured at 140 °C for 10 min. The polymerized PDMS layer was then carefully detached from the master before the use. A 0.42 M precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 106 mg of CsBr and 183.5 mg of PbBr2 (1:1 molar ratio) in 1.2 ml of dimethylsulfoxide. The mixture was stirred at 80 °C on a hotplate inside a nitrogen-filled glove box for 2 h, yielding a clear solution. Immediately before use, the precursor solution was diluted to concentrations in the range 0.05–0.1 M for the CsPbBr3 crystal growth. The precursor solution was deposited in contact with the patterned PDMS replica until the capillary pressure required for complete imbibition of the microstructures and nanostructures was reached. Once nucleation began, with the liquid meniscus pinned to the sidewalls of the nanoscale features, the PDMS replica was placed in conformal contact with a glass substrate to seal the microwire waveguides26,27. At this stage, capillary forces and surface interactions guided the solution through the microfluidic channels. Within the confined geometry, the reduced precursor volume and the progressively increasing concentration and viscosity gradients promoted perovskite nucleation through surface-tension-driven self-assembly precisely at the elastomer–air interface of each microstructure and nanostructure28,49,50,51. Crystallization inside the microchannels was optimized by imposing controlled temperature ramps (from 4 °C to room temperature) and by maintaining controlled vapour saturation and a pressure of 0.02 N cm−2 (refs. 52,53). After complete solvent evaporation, the PDMS replica was removed, yielding CsPbBr3 positive structures directly on the glass substrate that faithfully reproduced the microscale and nanoscale features of the original Si master. To assess fabrication reproducibility, we report in Supplementary Fig. 23 a set of nominally identical microwire arrays fabricated under the same conditions. The samples indicated a consistent optical response, with only minor detuning variations. It is vital to note that the grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width, see Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, to preserve continuous sidewalls in the elastomeric microchannels used for soft-lithography growth, ensuring uniform capillary filling and crystallization conditions while avoiding sidewall discontinuities that could introduce structural defects or make the crystal more fragile during replica peeling. The accessible limits of the proposed fabrication approach were determined by the fidelity of pattern transfer from the master mould to the elastomeric replica and subsequently to the perovskite crystal. On the basis of the aspect ratios demonstrated here (0.01–0.6), we anticipate that perovskite waveguides with thicknesses of roughly 100–150 nm and lateral dimensions of roughly 250–400 nm should be feasible. For periodic nanostructures, we note that some of the geometries investigated in this work (Supplementary Fig. 2) already contain lateral features as small as 50–80 nm, approaching the practical resolution limit of standard PDMS-based replication. Further reduction of the feature size would probably require optimization of the elastomeric replica itself.

Confocal images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope in high-resolution mode (1,024 × 1,024 pixel). Samples were prepared on microscope slides and characterized using a 488-nm excitation laser and a main beam splitter (MBS 488/639-nm) with appropriate photomultiplier tube (PMT) and gallium arsenide phosphide (GaAsP) detectors. All samples were imaged at various magnifications using Plan-Apochromat objectives of ×10 with a numerical aperture of NA = 0.45, ×20 NA = 0.8 and ×40 NA = 0.95. Three-dimensional images were obtained using the Z-stack scanning mode, which generated optical slices at various depths. Image analysis across different acquisition channels, tomographic reconstructions, spectral profiles and three-dimensional rendering were performed using the dedicated ZEN BLUE software.

AFM measurements were performed with a Dimension Icon (Bruker AXS) instrument, equipped with the Nanoscope V controller. Images were acquired in air, at room temperature, in Tapping Mode to protect the samples from damage. A rotated tapping etched silicon probe (Bruker) with a nominal radius of curvature R ≤ 8 nm was used. The morphology of the Si masters was investigated using a Sigma 300 (Zeiss) field emission SEM operated at an acceleration voltage of 5 kV and with an in-lens detector.

All the optical measurements were performed by using microscope objectives at ×100 magnification and a numerical aperture of 0.9 (Zeiss) in a reflection configuration. The pumping lasers were taken from a pulsed source (Pharos, Light Conversion) with a tunable repetition rate and a pulse duration of <290 fs, which drove two computer-controlled optical parametric amplifier (OPA) stages (Orpheus OPA, Light Conversion). The OPA outputs were independently tunable in wavelength and, depending on the specific measurement (single-beam or double-beam excitation), were used either simultaneously or individually. In all the experiments, the repetition rate was set to 10 kHz. Energy-resolved momentum-space maps were collected by imaging the back focal plane of the objective onto the entrance of a spectrometer (Andor, Kymera 328i Spectrograph), equipped with three gratings (150 lines per mm, 300 lines per mm, 600 lines per mm) and coupled to a two-dimensional charge-coupled device (CCD camera, Andor, iStar 334T). For photoluminescence off the resonance pump, the laser was set to 480 nm and the emitted photoluminescence signal was filtered using an edgepass filter (Thorlabs, FELH0500) to suppress the residual excitation laser and isolate the emission. TE and TM polarizations were defined with the waveguide axis aligned to the entrance slits of the spectrometer, such that the electric field was parallel (TE) or perpendicular (TM) to the grating periodicity. The two polarizations were selectively monitored by using a half-wave plate (AHWP10M-600) and a linear polarizer (GTH10M-A) along the detection line. The laser pumping power was controlled by using a variable neutral-density wheel filter. For double-beam experiments, the two OPA outputs were temporally matched by using a delay line (Newport, M-ILS 150CC DC Servo Linear Stage). Reflectivity measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 5 were performed by using a broadband white-light illumination in a reflection configuration, with a spot diameter of roughly 10 μm on the grating coupler. For the photoluminescence measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 7, the waveguide was excited between two gratings whereas for Supplementary Fig. 6 the emission from a single grating was spatially selected. With reference to Fig. 3b, the temporal profiles were obtained by subtracting the residual photoluminescence signal generated by the amplifier alone, which remained constant across all temporal scans. The amplifier-only signal was collected separately using the same exposure time and then subtracted from the measurements in which both beams were simultaneously present. The same procedure was applied to the measurements in Fig. 4c,d, for which the signal obtained with the phase shifter alone was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from the corresponding datasets. For the amplification measurements, Δt = 0 ps is defined as the relative amplifier-signal delay that maximizes the amplified signal intensity at the pumped region. This delay was experimentally optimized at each amplifier power, thereby inherently accounting for the relaxation dynamics leading to the population responsible for amplification and their possible dependence on the amplifier power.

It has been revealed that infinitely periodic dispersions have been calculated taking into account fully dispersive experimental literature values for the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index54. To quantitatively relate the measured phase difference to a microscopic excitonic energy shift, we consider two waveguides governed by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one of them subjected to a small blueshift of the exciton resonance. To relate to this experiment, this blueshift came from the interaction between the signal and the reservoir created by the non-resonant pump. The system was probed at a fixed frequency (ω), such that the effect of the perturbation would not change the frequency of the mode, but rather modify its propagation constant. The observable phase difference after a propagation length L therefore directly reflected the difference in wavevectors between the two configurations, (Δɸ = ΔkL). We consider the propagation of a waveguided mode in the strong-coupling regime described by the lower polariton dispersion relation. For a reference waveguide, the dispersion reads:.

In a recent development, here k denotes the in-plane wavevector (propagation constant) of the guided mode and c represents the slope of the bare photonic dispersion, such that \({E}_{{\rm{ph}}}(k)\approx {ck}\). The parameter Ω corresponds to the Rabi splitting energy whereas ωx is the exciton resonance energy. 📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (452 w)

Breaking: Donnarumma ‘aware’ of recent mistakes, insists Maresca

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Soccernews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.
  • Enzo Maresca insisted Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma is "aware" of his recent mistakes and revealed he will start against Fulham.
  • City lost each of their last three Premier League matches before the international break, a run which started with a 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Enzo Maresca insisted Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma is "aware" of his recent mistakes and revealed he will start against Fulham.

City lost each of their last three Premier League matches before the international break, a run which started with a 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa.

Donnarumma's mistake in that fixture led to Jackson's winner; only Bart Verbruggen (five), Jan Paul van Hecke and Robin Roefs (both four) have made more errors leading to goals than Donnarumma in the Premier League since the start of 2025-26.

And among goalkeepers, only Robin Roefs (eight) has committed more errors leading to goals in the competitions than Donnarumma (seven) in that time.

Donnarumma also made an error in Italy's Nations League win over France, before conceding four in a defeat to Belgium.

Maresca admitted City must stop their mistakes in defence, but believes Donnarumma will learn from his errors.

Sources indicate that "He has been good. With Italy he made the mistake in the build-up, but then I read that he was man of the match in the [next] game, he made many good saves," mentioned Maresca.

Hard work ahead of matchday  #AsahiSuperDry https://t.co/SGB849F2Rh.

— Manchester City (@ManCity) November 20, 2026.

It has been revealed that "Again, we made some mistakes in the last games and Gigio was part of that. He is aware and hopefully he's not going to make any more mistakes. He is going to start [against Fulham].

"In this moment, for sure, we are conceding too many goals. Most of them, from my point of view, are avoidable.

According to recent reports, "The idea is to continue to attack in the same way, creating chances and try to find a balance when we defend or when we are building [an attack]. If we can avoid mistakes, it's always better.".

City have won their last 20 games against Fulham in all competitions, the longest winning streak one team has had against another in English football.

However, City have lost each of their last three Premier League games, as many as in their previous 36 (W25 D8); since the start of 2007-08, they have only lost four in a row twice, doing so in August 2008 and December 2024.

Latest Update: Man United predicted lineup vs. Liverpool: Mauricio Pochettino makes Lisandro Martinez decision

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 16:39.
  • Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino could recall Lisandro Martinez to his starting lineup for his opening game in charge away to Liverpool on Sunday in the Premier League.
  • The Argentine defender is available to his compatriot after completing a domestic suspension and could now slot back into the rearguard alongside Harry Maguire, who has seemingly shaken off a back problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 16:39.

Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino could recall Lisandro Martinez to his starting lineup for his opening game in charge away to Liverpool on Sunday in the Premier League.

The Argentine defender is available to his compatriot after completing a domestic suspension and could now slot back into the rearguard alongside Harry Maguire, who has seemingly shaken off a back problem.

Noussair Mazraoui would be the most likely to make way if Martinez returns, as Leny Yoro shuffles over to right-back, on the opposite side to the much-maligned Diogo Dalot.

The Portugal international's withdrawal was cheered by fans in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, but with Patrick Dorgu operating in a more attack-minded role of late and Luke Shaw still doubtful, Dalot should reprise his role.

The same goes for Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo in the middle, as Pochettino sticks to a 4-2-3-1 setup for his maiden match and forces Andrey Santos to wait his turn.

The front four of Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo is likely to remain the same too, although Marcus Rashford (hip) is on the verge of returning and could be an option on Merseyside.

Carlos Baleba (hamstring), Manuel Ugarte (knee) and Benjamin Sesko (calf) all remain out of contention for the away side.

Manchester United possible starting lineup:.

Lammens; Yoro, Martinez, Maguire, Dalot; Tielemans, Mainoo; Diallo, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo.

  • Serie A's Sunday night showdown will see a battle of the Nerazzurri, as Atalanta BC welcome Inter Milan to Bergamo.
  • When the black-and-blue pair go toe to toe once again, the hosts hope to finally end an eight-year wait for victory over their regional rivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 20 Nov 2026 17:02, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:52.

Serie A's Sunday night showdown will see a battle of the Nerazzurri, as Atalanta BC welcome Inter Milan to Bergamo.

When the black-and-blue pair go toe to toe once again, the hosts hope to finally end an eight-year wait for victory over their regional rivals.

Having suffered derby defeat and slipped off top spot in Serie A, reigning champions Inter bounced back with two massive wins - and a rare pair of clean sheets - before international football intervened.

Responding to their Derby della Madonnina loss to old foes AC Milan, the Nerazzurri recorded a crucial Champions League victory against Feyenoord, then extended their long reign of dominance over Como.

The visitors were flying high following their own European exploits, but Inter put in a commanding display while posting a 15th consecutive Serie A home win over the Lariani.

Though surprise leaders Lazio finally dropped points, that was not quite enough to reclaim the summit, and Cristian Chivu's side went into the break sandwiched between both Rome clubs.

Now, they return to action with an crucial double-header, at home to Stuttgart in the Champions League and against Atalanta this weekend.

After nine consecutive away wins helped them secure the Scudetto last season, Inter's form on the road has recently faltered - relatively speaking, at least.

Nonetheless, the second-city giants have prevailed on all of their last four trips to Bergamo, averaging two goals per game.

In fact, Atalanta are winless across the last 15 league meetings at any venue, while also suffering defeats in the cup and Supercoppa Italiana.

Even during the golden Gian Piero Gasperini era, La Dea struggled to conquer Inter, picking up just two points from the last seven clashes on home turf.

This time, the pair will convene with Atalanta trailing far behind their Lombardy neighbours, languishing inside the bottom half of Serie A.

A 1-0 win over Monza somewhat steadied the ship ahead of the international break, after losing half of their first 10 league fixtures under Maurizio Sarri.

It also halted a streak of 11 games without a clean sheet, including in the Conference League, where the Bergamaschi only sit 16th halfway through the league phase.

Sarri's side have conceded the third-most shots in Italy's top tier, and already shipping 20 goals by this stage of a campaign represents Atalanta's worst defensive start since 2002.

All of which makes for grim reading ahead of Inter's visit to New Balance Arena, where the hosts have registered just four wins from nine games this term.

Atalanta BC form (all competitions):.

Inter Milan form (all competitions):.

Inter star Lautaro Martinez has scored in five of his last six league games against Atalanta, and he is set to return from an injury layoff on Sunday evening; only Aleksandar Stankovic and Ange Bonny are right now sidelined.

In his captain's absence, Marcus Thuram certainly stepped up, and a recent strike against Como took the French forward onto six Serie A goals for the season.

Pio Esposito also found the net in that match, ending a domestic drought that dated back to September; then, he hit the target twice before missing a penalty for Italy during an eventful international period.

Like Esposito, Atalanta's Nikola Krstovic scored in a 1-1 draw when these sides last met. The Montenegro striker is now in top form: the winner against Monza was his seventh league goal of the season, and he has just scored three times in two UEFA Nations League matches.

La Dea's injury list features three defenders - Isak Hien, Odilon Kossounou and Thomas Kristensen - while midfielder Gianluca Gaetano remains a doubt.

More positively for Sarri, ex-Inter wing-back Raoul Bellanova and Italy forward Giacomo Raspadori are both back in contention after recovering from thigh problems.

Atalanta BC possible starting lineup:.

Carnesecchi; Zappacosta, Scalvini, Kolasinac, Bernasconi; Ederson, Kessie; Elmas, De Ketelaere, Rowe; Krstovic.

Inter Milan possible starting lineup:.

J. Martinez; Bisseck, Akanji, Bastoni; Spence, Barella, Calhanoglu, Jones, Dimarco; Thuram, Esposito.

Inter have attempted the most shots in Serie A this season, they last failed to score in March, and their prolific talisman is set to make his long-awaited comeback.

That could mean trouble for Atalanta's fragile defence, so the hosts will suffer yet another defeat to their Nerazzurro neighbours.

By IAN LADYMAN, FOOTBALL EDITOR.

When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

Recent findings suggest that rangnick replied that he was certain it could. The German was, of course, proved very wrong.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

Recent findings suggest that heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

Recent findings suggest that but no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

According to recent reports, this United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

In a recent development, mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford.

This United squad is not one built for the latest United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football.

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

Recent findings suggest that the good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

In a recent development, son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

In a recent development, ‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

According to recent reports, ‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’.

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players.

It has been revealed that 'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' notes Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’.

The physical limitations of this United team were clear in the titanic but ultimately rather pitiful 4-4 draw with Aston Villa that proved to be Michael Carrick’s last game in charge just before the international break.

It has been revealed that invited back into a game they trailed 2-0, United’s front four briefly chased the life out of Villa when Unai Emery’s team were in possession. For 20 minutes, Villa could not get out of their own half.

But the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

According to recent reports, at Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

Recent findings suggest that six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ stated former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’.

It has been revealed that trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

In a recent development, 'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ says Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’.

For this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

Sources indicate that at United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

It has been revealed that equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather latest. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather newly introduced when he landed at Southampton in 2013.

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

In a recent development, there is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

This, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three notes everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

Pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as important as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

In a recent development, ‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’.

Sources indicate that pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He mentioned, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’.

It has been revealed that equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

At Tottenham, Pochettino would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in.

Industry observers note that pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment.

It has been revealed that as strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

Recent findings suggest that these are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like upcoming-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

Industry observers note that ‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave New World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’.

What manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a new manager bounce at Old Trafford.

According to recent reports, his relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their fresh boss.

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea.

In a recent development, united’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

According to recent reports, so, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

It has been revealed that here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

Pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

According to recent reports, the man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

In a recent development, but Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate concerns, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.
  • This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic.
  • The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

It has been revealed that the best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

In a recent development, “I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman mentioned. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”.

Recent findings suggest that avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

Industry observers note that it did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

She is an exciting player for the future but will feel she has a chance of making a World Cup squad, should England get there. For now, they are taking the slow route.

“I do [like playing that position], I love defending as well. It’s obviously a bit different for me up there but I always try and give my best whatever position I play so I did enjoy it.”.

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”.

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

According to recent reports, “When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman noted. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

According to recent reports, “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”.

Toone rapidly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”.

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca faces an urgent tactical puzzle ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham, as glaring structural flaws in his revamped midfield continue to leave the Sky Blues dangerously exposed on the counter-attack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 17:09.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca faces an urgent tactical puzzle ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham, as glaring structural flaws in his revamped midfield continue to leave the Sky Blues dangerously exposed on the counter-attack.

After kicking off his tenure at the Etihad Stadium with seven consecutive Premier League victories, the Italian has since overseen a jarring slump, suffering three straight top-flight defeats, most recently losing 3-1 at Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.

While City's off-pitch turbulence regarding their financial charges case has dominated headlines, their recent on-pitch struggles stem largely from a £300m+ summer engine-room overhaul that has yet to find its rhythm.

Specifically, Maresca is grappling with how to integrate his two marquee £100m-plus acquisitions – Enzo Fernandez and Elliot Anderson – without sacrificing defensive solidity.

It has been revealed that throughout the opening months of the 2026-27 campaign, Man City have looked remarkably fragile whenever possession turns over. Only Newcastle United (20) have allowed more shots from fast breaks in the Premier League this term than the Citizens (17), who were sliced open repeatedly at the City Ground.

In that defeat to Forest, Maresca's side conceded eight fast breaks – the highest single-game tally by any top-flight club this season – and shipped two goals directly from rapid transitions.

According to recent reports, the core problem lies in the incompatible profiles of Maresca's preferred central trio. Deploying Anderson alongside Fernandez in a double pivot behind playmaker Rayan Cherki creates a vacuum when City lose the ball.

Cherki contributes very little defensively, which places an unsustainable burden on the two deeper midfielders to screen the backline.

Rather than operating as a cohesive unit, Fernandez and Anderson frequently occupy the same right-sided zones, leaving the central and left-sided areas of the pitch wide open.

Premier League per-90 metrics (2025-26 vs. 2026-27).

Furthermore, Fernandez's defensive output has dipped noticeably since his £125m move from Chelsea; his tackle and possession-win rates per 90 minutes are down, while he struggled to impose himself physically against Forest.

While Forest duo Xaver Schlager and Ryan Yates dominated the battleground with 14 and 11 defensive contributions respectively, Fernandez managed just four – one fewer than Cherki (five).

Speaking at his pre-match press conference on Friday afternoon, Maresca was quick to shield his Argentine international from individual blame while acknowledging that tactical tweaks are required to restore equilibrium across the pitch.

"We won games with Enzo on the pitch," Maresca told reporters. "I know when there is a defeat we are all looking forward for the reason why and sometimes we think it's this or that.

Industry observers note that "Sometimes probably we need more balance, different players on the pitch. It depends on the game. But we won games with Enzo, we lost games with Enzo. It's not just Enzo.

In a recent development, "But we are going to find solutions for more balance on the defensive line, in midfield and up front. I can't control what we pay for the players. People can think he's not going to make any mistake ever. He's a human being and he is going to make some mistakes.".

With Pep Guardiola's former side having lost key control-oriented figures like Bernardo Silva and Rodri over the summer, Maresca cannot simply replicate his predecessor's blueprint. However, he does have the personnel to inject much-needed steel into his spine.

The most straightforward adjustment involves handing a bigger role to teenage summer arrival Ayyoub Bouaddi, who is widely regarded as one of the brightest young prospects in world football.

Restricted to just 177 Premier League minutes so far (two starts, three substitute outings) while adapting to English football, the athletic youngster offers the natural positional discipline and ball-winning instincts of a true holding number six.

Pairing the Moroccan ace with Anderson at the base of City’s midfield would help relieve the defensive strain on the England international and plug the gaps that several Premier League teams have ruthlessly exploited.

Sources indicate that crucially, introducing Bouaddi does not require banishing Fernandez to the substitutes' bench. Having pushed hard to bring the 25-year-old to Manchester just over two months ago, Maresca could instead move Fernandez further forward to operate at the apex of a midfield triangle in place of Cherki.

Fernandez’s ability to hold up play, draw fouls, time late runs into the penalty area and thread incisive passes makes him well-suited to an advanced role – provided he has two disciplined ball-winners anchoring the space behind him.

Man City enter Saturday's fixture boasting an extraordinary 20-match winning streak against Fulham in all competitions, having scored at least twice in every single one of those victories, yet memories of last season's chaotic 5-4 escape at Craven Cottage serve as a timely warning.

If Maresca fails to tighten his midfield structure this weekend, Man City's concerning vulnerability on the break threatens to derail their season before winter truly sets in.

Emotional Mauricio Pochettino gets perfect sendoff in his US farewell... before boarding jet for fresh life as Manchester United manager
